newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to consider more food aid for N.Korea.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to consider more food aid for N.Korea.

text.p: The United States said on Thursday it would consider providing additional food aid to North Korea on humanitarian grounds but declined to tie aid directly to a deal for Korean peninsula peace talks.

"The United States ... has no plans at this time to provide additional food aid to North Korea. We continue to monitor the situation closely. We will consider future appeals for food aid. But ... we contribute food aid based on humanitarian needs," State Department spokesman John Dinger told reporters.

"We have from the beginning provided the food aid and humanitarian assistance ... based on humanitarian needs, not linked to political developments. And that is how we intend to continue," Dinger said.

He was responding to comments by South Korean officials in Seoul who reported that impoverished North Korea has agreed to join proposed four-nation peace talks if the United States and South Korea first guaranteed food aid.

A South Korean foreign ministry spokesman told Reuters in Seoul: "North Korea asked the United States and South Korea to guarantee food aid in advance...You could say it was a conditional acceptance of the proposal."
He added: "We have repeated our position that food aid can be discussed in the four-party talks in the framework of easing tension and building peace. The United States maintains the same stand."

Dinger confirmed the United States, South Korea and North Korea held a working level meeting in New York on Wednesday on a U.S.-South Korean proposal for negotiations on a permanent peace for the Korean peninsula that would also include China.
The meeting was a follow up to a briefing Washington and Seoul gave the North on March 5 on the peace talks proposal.

But Dinger insisted: "No agreement of any sort was reached at yesterday's meeting. We understand (North Korea) is still considering our proposal ... And we hope the DPRK will agree soon to four-party talks."

He said in the New York meeting North Korea "did raise, as expected, its severe food shortage situation" and he stressed the United States appreciated the severity of the problem and has donated food aid in the past, including recently.

His comments seemed designed to make clear that while Washington was opposed to linking food aid directly with a political deal for peace talks, it remained concerned about Pyongyang's food shortages and opened to providing food aid when and if warranted.

In addition to preserving a principle of not using food as a political weapon, the Clinton adminstration may be worried about appearing to make too many concessions in order to just get the Stalinist regime to the peace table.
The United States and South Korea have said food aid can be discussed when the peace talks begin.
International aid agencies say North Korea, devastated by two consecutive years of floods, is weeks away from starvation.
The State Department said no further U.S.-South Korea talks are planned but the parties often do not announce their meetings in advance.
U.S. Vice President Al Gore was due in Seoul on Friday on the last leg of a tour of Asia and was expected to discuss ways to lure Pyongyang to the talks.

The four participants would be the United States, the two Koreas and China, a long-time ally of the North. The aim of the talks is to forge a lasting peace to replace a truce agreement that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
